01-reality-of-ownership.title: The owner who bought twice.
01-reality-of-ownership.standfirst: He sold the first yacht eighteen months after delivery, took the loss, and started again. The second yacht was a better acquisition because the first had shown him what ownership costs and who was being paid by whom.

meta.label: Anonymisation
meta.value: Composite of three Foreland project files. Quoted remarks are representative of the files, not verbatim

paragraphs: The buyer was in his early fifties, recently exited from a software business he had founded in 2003. The sale left him with cash in the low nine figures. Yachting had been a deferred ambition since university. The first acquisition, made within ten months of the exit, was a semi-custom 42 m motor yacht from a respected mid-tier yard, sourced through a brokerage relationship introduced by his wealth manager.

The brokerage handled the search, the contract, the surveyor referral, and the management company onboarding. The brokerage’s fees did not appear on the buyer’s invoices because the seller paid them. He understood, vaguely, that the broker was being paid by the seller. He did not understand that the broker had also recommended the surveyor, the management company, and the captain, and that the brokerage could earn referral fees from each of those engagements.

In the first year the family used the yacht for ten weeks in the Western Mediterranean. The captain, hired on the broker’s recommendation, ran a pleasant programme. Operating cost in year one came in at EUR 1.9 m, against a broker-quoted budget of EUR 1.3 m. Crew salaries were higher than expected. Insurance was higher. The yard period after the first season brought a EUR 280,000 invoice for snag-list items the buyer had assumed were within the warranty window. They were not, because the contract, on standard terms, ran the warranty for twelve months from delivery, not from the end of the first season.

The captain explained that operating cost on a yacht of this size was typically around 10 percent of value. The buyer noted that EUR 1.9 m on an EUR 11 m hull was 17 percent. The captain was reassuring. The buyer was not.

The family used the yacht for eight weeks in year two. By then the buyer had begun to suspect that the people he had taken on with the first purchase were not working for him. He engaged independent counsel for an unrelated tax matter, and the lawyer asked, in passing, who had drafted his original purchase contract. The buyer named the firm. The lawyer noted that the firm was the brokerage’s preferred counsel. The buyer had not asked the question.

He commissioned an independent review of his operating arrangements. The review found that the management company paid EUR 200,000 a year in referral fees to the brokerage that had introduced them. The buyer had not been told about this. He had not been told because there was no rule that compelled the management company to disclose referrals it pays to its yacht-owning client. The review found similar referral payments on the insurance arrangement, the paint contract scoped for the next refit, and the recruitment fees on the recent crew rotation.
None of this was illegal, and none of it was unusual by the standards of the industry.

paragraphs.text: I had assumed the people around the yacht were working for me. They were working in the industry. The two are different.
paragraphs.attribution: A remark representative of the buyers in the three files, year two.

paragraphs.text: The decision to sell, and the second acquisition

paragraphs: The decision to sell the first yacht was taken at the end of the second season. The yacht went onto the brokerage market and sold within four months for EUR 3.1 m less than he had paid, a loss of 28 percent. Broker-published figures put the loss in the first year of ownership at 10 to 20 percent; selling quickly, at the price the market offered, cost him more. Operating cost across the two seasons was approximately EUR 4 m. Brokerage commission and other costs of the sale added approximately EUR 0.8 m. The total cost of the first 18 months was approximately EUR 8 m.

The second acquisition was organised differently from the start. He engaged an independent adviser before contacting any broker. The adviser briefed him on the acquisition process, on who in the industry is paid by whom, and on the team he would need. The adviser ran the search across several brokerages, evaluated three shortlisted yachts, checked yachts for sale privately but not listed, and recommended an independent surveyor and a yacht lawyer he had no commercial relationship with.

The second yacht, a 46 m semi-custom from a higher-tier yard, took eight months to acquire from first conversation to closing. The buyer paid the independent adviser USD 180,000 for the year of work. He paid the lawyer USD 90,000 for the contract negotiation. He paid the surveyor USD 45,000 for a four-day pre-purchase survey. The total team cost was approximately USD 320,000 on a USD 24 m acquisition. He had paid nothing equivalent on the first yacht, which had cost him approximately EUR 8 m in 18 months.

The buyer is now in his fifth year with the second yacht. The crew has stayed largely intact across four years; the captain is the same one hired through an independent recruitment process at the start. Operating cost has run at 13 to 14 percent of original capex per year, within the range for moderate use that the adviser had set out at the start.
The buyer is unlikely to sell. He is also unlikely, on this yacht, to be surprised by an invoice. The costs have matched the budget he was given, and he pays the team directly at known rates.
takeaways: Engage an independent adviser before engaging any broker. In this case the choice of advisers made more difference to cost than the choice of yacht.
Operating cost in years one to three is more often 12 to 17 percent of capex than the 10 percent rule of folklore.
Referral payments from management companies, paint contractors, insurers and crew agencies to the introducing broker are routine. They do not appear on your invoice, so ask about them explicitly.
An independent adviser, lawyer and surveyor on a USD 30 m acquisition cost about USD 200 to 400 k in year one. The wrong team can cost several percent of the purchase price.
01-reality-of-ownership.disclosure: This case is a composite of three Foreland Marine project files. Identifying details, jurisdictions, and figures have been adjusted to protect the parties involved. The cost outcomes, and the way each advisory team was engaged and paid, are accurate to the original projects.

01-reality-of-ownership.seoDescription: A first-time buyer sold 18 months after delivery and started again. What the first purchase cost him, and what the second one got right.

02-reading-the-market.title: The buyer who walked away, and the buyer who closed.
02-reading-the-market.standfirst: This illustration sets two 2025 transactions on one 52 m brokerage yacht. One buyer had an adviser and kept to a ceiling price set in advance. The other accepted the listing broker’s account of urgency and paid 5 to 11 percent more than the adviser’s estimate of fair value.

meta.label: Outcome, buyer B
meta.value: Closed at EUR 27.8 m, 5 to 11 percent above the adviser’s estimate of fair value

meta.label: Anonymisation
meta.value: Composite of two 2025 transactions, set on one yacht for comparison. Quoted remarks are representative of the files, not verbatim

paragraphs: This case combines two 2025 transactions involving first-time buyers. So that the two can be compared, both are set here on the same yacht: a 52 m motor yacht on the brokerage market, listed at EUR 32 m fourteen months earlier and reduced three times since, to EUR 28 m.

Buyer A engaged an independent adviser before contacting the listing broker. The adviser took the listing’s history from public broker portals, compared three other 50 to 55 m yachts of similar age and yard, and checked the yacht’s time on the market against the most recent published median for its size band. The comparison suggested a fair price of EUR 25 to 26.5 m. Fourteen months on the market and three price cuts showed that no buyer had been found at the earlier asking prices. The adviser recommended an opening offer of EUR 24.5 m and a ceiling of EUR 26.5 m.

Buyer B did not engage an independent adviser. The listing broker introduced him to the yacht and told him that it was likely to sell soon, that another buyer was close to an offer and that prices in the segment were rising. The yacht’s record did not support that account: it had been cut three times in fourteen months, and prices in the segment had eased from their peak.

Buyer A opened at EUR 24.5 m. The seller countered at EUR 27.5 m. Buyer A raised the offer to EUR 25.5 m, then to EUR 26.5 m. The seller would not go below EUR 27.5 m within the time the buyer had allowed, and Buyer A withdrew on the adviser’s recommendation. The adviser’s view was that the seller’s price did not reflect the yacht’s record on the market, and that the buyer should not go above the ceiling agreed in advance.

Buyer B offered the asking price of EUR 28 m. The broker suggested asking for a small reduction and closing quickly, and Buyer B closed at EUR 27.8 m. On the MYBA scale the commission at that price is about EUR 1.7 m, paid by the seller. The buyer-side share, around EUR 850,000, went to a broker who had not acted for Buyer B in any practical sense.

Four months after withdrawing, Buyer A bought a different 50 m yacht for EUR 25.2 m. It had a different layout but suited the same kind of cruising, and its build quality, from a different mid-tier yard, was comparable.

Buyer B’s yacht was offered for charter in its first season under his ownership, generated EUR 750,000 in net charter revenue against EUR 2.1 m in operating cost, and was relisted in early 2026 at EUR 24.5 m.

Buyer A had access to the same data Buyer B did. Both buyers could have pulled the listing’s history from broker portals. Both could have run a comparable scan. The difference was that Buyer A had engaged an adviser whose only job was to judge the price on the buyer’s behalf. Buyer B dealt only with the listing broker, whose job was to close the transaction for the seller.
takeaways: Days-on-market and price-reduction history are public on listing portals. Read the data before acting on a broker’s account of urgency.
A hull on the market for 14 months with three price cuts is evidence that the asking price is above what buyers will pay. A buyer with a ceiling price agreed in advance can walk away.
On a single transaction, advice on price alone can save more than an adviser’s annual fee.
A broker’s report that another buyer is “about to offer” is not market evidence on its own; ask what it rests on.

The two transactions are set here on one yacht so that they can be compared. Identifying details adjusted; figures kept within their original ranges.

03-how-the-industry-works.title: The free advice that cost GBP 320,000.
03-how-the-industry-works.standfirst: The buyer was offered “free” guidance by a brokerage on the management contract, the paint specialist, the insurance broker, and the recruitment agency. Each firm introduced paid the brokerage a referral fee or retrocession he was not told about. He saved approximately GBP 75,000 in advisory fees. The payments to the brokerage in year one came to approximately GBP 320,000.

meta.label: Anonymisation
meta.value: Composite of two Foreland project files, 2024. Quoted remarks are representative of the files, not verbatim

paragraphs: The buyer was UK-based, recently exited from a private equity holding, considering a first acquisition in the 35 to 40 m band. He approached a major London brokerage on the recommendation of a peer who had bought through them. The brokerage waived its buyer-side advisory fee on the basis that the firm earned its margin on the seller side and “provided buyer support as part of the relationship.” The wording is common across the industry.

The acquisition itself ran cleanly. A 38 m semi-custom motor yacht from an Italian yard was sourced over four months. The pre-purchase survey was conducted by a surveyor the broker introduced. The contract was drafted by the broker’s preferred yacht lawyer. The yacht closed at EUR 19 m, on terms slightly more favourable than the asking. The buyer felt well-served.

Once closed, the buyer needed a management company, a paint specialist for an early refit on the bow, an insurance broker, and senior crew. The brokerage made the introductions. Each was warm, professional, and competent.

The management company was a recognised industry firm, contracted to run an annual operating budget of EUR 2.8 m. The buyer was told, accurately, that the management fee was at market rate. He was not told that the brokerage held a referral relationship with the management company. The introductory referral, 10 percent of the year-one budget and paid by the management company, was EUR 280,000, approximately GBP 240,000.

The paint specialist was selected from a list of three the brokerage maintained. The chosen contractor delivered a EUR 1.8 m repaint job. A 5 percent retrocession back to the brokerage on this job was approximately EUR 90,000, about GBP 76,000. The buyer paid the paint contractor in full, and none of the retrocession appeared on the buyer’s invoices.

The insurance broker was a relationship of long standing for the brokerage. Premium in year one was approximately EUR 250,000. Brokerage commission on the policy was approximately 15 percent (EUR 37,500). A back-end referral fee from the insurance broker to the introducing brokerage was approximately 10 percent of that commission, or EUR 3,750. Small, but recurring annually.

The recruitment agency that placed the new captain charged a placement fee of approximately three months of the captain’s salary, around EUR 35,000. The agency paid the brokerage a referral fee of around 10 percent of that fee. The buyer was charged the full agency fee.

The buyer had “saved” an explicit advisory fee by engaging the brokerage as his de facto adviser. A typical independent adviser fee on this acquisition would have been around USD 80,000 to 120,000. He had saved approximately GBP 75,000 in explicit fees.

Across year one alone, the referral fees and retrocessions paid by his suppliers to the introducing brokerage came to approximately GBP 320,000: about GBP 240,000 on the management contract, GBP 76,000 on the repaint, and about GBP 3,000 each on the insurance and recruitment referrals. None was illegal or unusual in the industry, and none appeared on the buyer’s invoices, because the payments passed between the suppliers and the brokerage.

The advice had not been free. Its cost was carried in the prices of the suppliers the brokerage had introduced. The buyer had paid for the advice at a multiple of what an independent adviser would have charged, and in each case had been steered to the brokerage’s commercial partners rather than given an independent comparison of the market.

The buyer engaged an independent adviser at the end of year one for an unrelated assessment of his refit reserve planning. The adviser, on reviewing the operating arrangements, found the referral payments. The buyer was not, in the end, particularly outraged. He understood the arrangement once it was explained; he had simply not been told about it. He renegotiated the management contract at year two with a clear understanding of the cost base, moved the insurance to a broker with no relationship to the original brokerage, and adjusted the recruitment process for future hires.

Year two operating cost, with the same suppliers on directly negotiated terms and full disclosure, and leaving the one-off repaint aside, was approximately GBP 240,000 lower than year one. The buyer concluded that the original arrangements had cost him about GBP 240,000 a year while they were in place, and about GBP 320,000 in year one with the repaint. He kept the yacht on the renegotiated terms.
takeaways: When a brokerage offers “free” buyer support, ask explicitly whether each firm they introduce pays them a referral fee or retrocession, and how much.

In this case the management company, the paint contractor, the insurance broker and the recruitment agency all paid the introducing brokerage. A payment that is not on your invoice can still be part of your costs.
An independent adviser fee of USD 80 to 120 k on a EUR 19 m acquisition is a fraction of the year-one referral payments in this case.
Renegotiating supplier relationships at year two, with full disclosure of the original referral payments, can be one of the largest cost reductions open to a first-year owner.

04-acquisition-process.title: The pre-purchase survey that saved EUR 2 m.
04-acquisition-process.standfirst: The seller was confident in the recent class survey. The buyer’s independent surveyor opened up two compartments the class surveyor had not. The renegotiation that followed reduced the price by EUR 2.1 m, and the buyer took on the remediation that the reduction paid for.
paragraphs: The yacht was a 55 m motor from a respected Northern European yard, nine years old, with a clean class history and a recent five-year survey. The seller had instructed the listing broker to market the yacht as turnkey and to discourage extensive pre-purchase scoping on the basis that “the class survey covered everything that mattered.” The asking price was EUR 22 m.

The buyer engaged an independent surveyor on the recommendation of his independent adviser, not on the recommendation of the broker. The surveyor’s scope was broader than the seller’s recent class survey: 6 days afloat, 2 days haul-out, full mechanical inspection by an independently engaged chief engineer, paint condition assessment, electrical compliance audit, and opening of two compartments the class surveyor had not opened (the forepeak void and a section of the lazarette adjacent to the stabiliser pumps).
The class survey had passed the yacht. The pre-purchase survey found problems the class survey had not recorded, of which three mattered most.

First, the forepeak void showed early-stage corrosion in the structural framing, consistent with prolonged moisture from a leaking deck fitting two decks above. The corrosion had not penetrated the primary structural members but the affected secondary framing was within five years of needing replacement. Estimated remediation cost: EUR 350,000 to 500,000.

Second, the lazarette opening revealed that the stabiliser pump installation had been modified, post-build, to accommodate an upgraded stabiliser system in 2019. The modification had been documented, and the documents showed that it had reduced the engine room ventilation. The ventilation had been running at approximately 80 percent of design capacity since 2019. Estimated remediation cost to restore design capacity: EUR 250,000 to 400,000.

Third, the surveyor’s mechanical inspection identified that one of the two main engines was due for major overhaul within 1,500 hours of operation. The seller’s broker had described the engines as “good for the next class period.” The next class renewal was five years away. 1,500 hours, at the yacht’s historical use, was about three years. The discrepancy was material. Estimated overhaul cost: EUR 800,000.

There was also a longer list of smaller findings (paint blisters in two locations, an autopilot due for replacement, a navigation electronics suite at the end of its support life). Total estimated remediation over the ten years the buyer planned to own the yacht: EUR 2.0 to 2.4 m.

The buyer’s lawyer drafted the request for a price reduction based on the survey. The argument was straightforward: the deficiencies were not catastrophic, but they were material, and the price needed to reflect them.

Three options were presented to the seller. One: walk away. Two: have the seller remediate at the seller’s expense before closing, with class re-inspection. Three: reduce the price by EUR 2.1 m to reflect the deficiencies.

The seller chose option three. The yacht closed at EUR 19.9 m. The buyer carried the remediation work into the first refit, sequencing it across the 18 months following acquisition. The total spend was within the EUR 2.0 to 2.4 m range the surveyor had estimated.

paragraphs.text: The cost of the survey against the price reduction

paragraphs: The independent surveyor’s fee was EUR 48,000. The independently engaged chief engineer’s fee was EUR 12,000. The lawyer’s fee for the renegotiation alone was approximately EUR 25,000. Total cost of the survey, the engineer’s inspection and the renegotiation: EUR 85,000.

The price reduction was EUR 2.1 m, about 25 times the EUR 85,000 the survey process cost. The reduction was not a profit: the buyer still spent EUR 2.0 to 2.4 m on remediation, which it roughly covered. Against closing at the asking price without the survey, the buyer was about EUR 2.0 m better off (EUR 2.1 m less EUR 85,000). On any acquisition above about EUR 5 m, the cost of an independent survey is small against what it can find.

What would have happened without the survey: the buyer would have closed at EUR 22 m and absorbed the EUR 2.0 to 2.4 m of remediation in the years that followed. He would have paid about EUR 2.0 m more in total than he did, after allowing for the EUR 85,000 the survey process cost. That sum would have stayed with the seller.
takeaways: Class surveys are not buyer-side surveys. They confirm that the yacht meets class requirements; they are not designed to protect a buyer.
An independent surveyor at USD 25 to 60 k on a 40 to 60 m yacht can return many times its fee, as it did here, though not every survey finds as much.
Open compartments the class surveyor has not opened. Set the survey scope by the buyer’s intended use, not by the seller’s assurances.
Material findings justify renegotiating the price. Walking away is the right answer when the seller will not move.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.title: The spec change in month 18.
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.standfirst: Eighteen months into a 36-month new build, the owner asked for a structural change to the upper deck. The change was technically straightforward, but the contract set no unit rates for variations and gave the owner no right to obtain other quotes. The yard charged EUR 1.4 m above its own engineering estimate.

meta.label: Anonymisation
meta.value: Composite of two Foreland project files, 2022 to 2024. Quoted remarks are representative of the files, not verbatim

paragraphs: This account combines two project files. The owner had committed to a 62 m fully custom new build at a top-tier Northern European yard. The contract at signature was EUR 95 m, against a 36-month build window. The owner had retained a brokerage acting in a dual role: the firm had introduced the yard, was acting as owner’s representative on the build, and was being paid by yard commission of approximately 5 percent. The owner had been told that this was the usual arrangement in the industry. Such arrangements are common.

The contract was the yard’s in-house template. The owner’s representative had reviewed it but had not been involved in its drafting. A specialist shipbuilding lawyer had not been engaged. The contract included a change order clause that specified, in general terms, that the yard would price variations at “reasonable cost plus a margin appropriate to the work.” The clause did not specify what reasonable cost meant, what margin was appropriate, or whether the buyer had the right to obtain third-party quotes for variations above a defined threshold.

Eighteen months in, with the hull complete and outfitting underway, the owner asked for a structural change to the upper deck to accommodate a tender lift the original specification had not anticipated. The change involved reinforcing two structural frames, modifying the deck cut-out, integrating the lift hydraulics, and re-running the deck drainage.

The yard’s change order quote was EUR 2.6 m. The yard’s engineering estimate, which the owner’s representative obtained informally, suggested the actual additional engineering, materials, and labour cost was approximately EUR 1.2 m. The yard’s margin on the change order was therefore approximately EUR 1.4 m, or about 117 percent on the underlying cost.

The owner, on the dual-role representative’s advice, accepted the change order. The representative advised that changes at this stage of a build always carry a premium, and that disputing the price would damage the relationship with the yard. Both points had some truth, but neither mentioned that the size of the premium followed from the contract terms.

The EUR 1.2 m of engineering, materials and labour would have been payable under any contract. The EUR 1.4 m margin was a different matter. A specialist shipbuilding lawyer would have negotiated pre-agreed unit rates and the right to obtain third-party quotes above a threshold at heads of terms, so that the yard’s price could be checked against the rates and against other bidders. Some margin would still have been payable, but the yard could not have set it alone. The owner had instead a general clause under which the yard would charge what it considered reasonable.

paragraphs.text: The owner is open to being forced to pay for change orders or emergent work at a unit rate much higher than in the original contract.
paragraphs.attribution: Sean Gibbons, Stephenson Harwood, on shipbuilding contract drafting.

paragraphs: The deck change was not the only variation. Across the remaining 18 months of the build, the owner approved 31 change orders totalling EUR 13 m above contract. Approximately 60 percent of those costs were the underlying engineering and materials. Approximately 40 percent was yard margin on the variations.

On a EUR 95 m contract that finished at EUR 108 m, the owner had paid approximately EUR 5.2 m in margin on variations (40 percent of EUR 13 m). The other EUR 7.8 m, the engineering and materials, would have been paid under any contract. Some margin is payable under any terms; unit rates and quote rights would have limited how much. The dual-role owner’s representative’s commission, paid by the yard, was approximately EUR 4.75 m on the original contract value, equal to about 90 percent of the variation margin paid by the owner.

The owner did not, at any stage, see an invoice from his representative. He paid the yard the contract value plus variations. The yard paid the representative’s commission out of its margin. As the owner saw it, the representative had cost him nothing.

paragraphs.text: The independent adviser brought in for delivery

paragraphs: Three months before delivery, with the yard pressing for sea trial scheduling and the snag list growing, the owner engaged an independent adviser to manage the acceptance process. The adviser ran the snag list, the sea trial, the technical handover, and the final acceptance protocol. The adviser’s fee was approximately EUR 180,000 across the four-month engagement.

The adviser’s assessment was that the change-order clause had allowed the yard about EUR 5.2 m in margin across the build, and that a representative paid by yard commission had had no financial reason to negotiate it differently. The owner accepted the analysis. The yacht was delivered on schedule, with a snag list managed to closure within four months of delivery.

The owner’s second build was contracted with a specialist shipbuilding lawyer at heads of terms, an independent owner’s representative paid solely by the owner, and a defined change order procedure with pre-agreed unit rates and third-party quote rights. Variation margin across that build was within the range practitioners regard as normal.
takeaways: The change order clause is among the most expensive new-build clauses to get wrong. Without defined unit rates and third-party quote rights, the yard sets the price of each variation.

Dual-role representation paid by yard commission is not free. In this case the commission was never set out in writing, and it was paid out of the yard’s margin, which the loose change-order clause allowed to grow.

Engage specialist shipbuilding counsel at heads of terms, not after the contract is signed. In this case the unconstrained clause cost about EUR 5.2 m in variation margin, more than an independent representative’s fee for the whole build.
The independent owner’s representative on a EUR 100 m build, paid 1 to 3 percent of build cost, costs EUR 1 to 3 m, less than the EUR 5.2 m paid in variation margin in this case.

06-refit.title: The refit that doubled in scope.
06-refit.standfirst: The owner committed to a EUR 3.2 m mid-life refit at a recognised Mediterranean yard. Once the yacht was opened up the yard found work that genuinely needed doing, and the final cost was double the original quote. The four main findings added EUR 1.37 m; the rest of the increase built up under a loosely defined scope, payments tied to calendar dates, and reporting that did not track cost against budget.

meta.label: Anonymisation
meta.value: Composite of two Foreland project files, 2022 to 2024. Quoted remarks are representative of the files, not verbatim

paragraphs: This account combines two project files. The yacht was 12 years old, approaching its second five-year survey, and its finishes and major systems needed substantial overhaul. The owner had bought the yacht two years earlier on the brokerage market and intended to hold it for another five years. The refit was the right decision in principle.

The yard chosen was a recognised Western Mediterranean operator, well-equipped, with a strong reputation for paint and structural work. The original quote was EUR 3.2 m for paint, deck refurbishment, an interior soft-furnishings refresh, mechanical service across both main engines and the generators, and electrical compliance work to address known issues from the previous five-year survey.

The contract was the yard’s standard refit agreement. The scope was specified in general terms across nine work packages. Milestone payments were tied to calendar dates rather than to defined deliverables. The owner’s representative was the brokerage that had sold the yacht to the owner two years earlier. The brokerage was paid no separate fee for the refit oversight, which it treated as part of its relationship with the owner.

paragraphs.text: What the yard found once work began

paragraphs: Five weeks into the project, with the engine room stripped, the yard’s mechanical team found that the port main engine’s heat exchanger had developed a cracked end cap, a defect that had not been visible from the engine’s service history. The crack was significant enough that the engine could not safely be re-started without full overhaul of the cooling system. The yard’s estimate for the additional work was EUR 380,000.

Three weeks later, the electrical compliance team found that the previous yard’s compliance work had been incomplete. Two switchboards had been left in a configuration that would not pass current class inspection. The remediation cost was EUR 220,000.

Four weeks later, the paint team found that the primer beneath the topsides had broken down in two locations, requiring full strip and re-prime before the new topcoat could be applied. The additional cost was EUR 480,000.

Six weeks later, the interior team found that the air handling units in two of the guest cabins had been running at reduced capacity for years and required complete replacement. The additional cost was EUR 290,000.

Each finding was genuine, of a kind commonly found once a yacht is opened up, and none could have been priced from the original visual inspection. The yard reported each one competently, and priced each on terms that suited the yard.

The owner’s representative attended on Tuesdays. The owner himself attended once a month for two days. The representative’s reports were largely descriptive, noting for example that a paint cell was complete or that engine work was continuing, without a quantified snag list against original scope or a running variance against budget.

By month four, the project was at EUR 4.6 m, against the EUR 3.2 m original quote. The owner asked the representative for a fixed final cost. The representative offered EUR 5.0 m. By month seven, the project was at EUR 5.8 m. By month nine, it was at EUR 6.1 m. The project finished at EUR 6.4 m, double the original quote, four months past the planned redelivery.

An overrun of 100 percent is at the high end of practitioner experience, but not unique. Of the EUR 3.2 m increase, the four findings above account for EUR 1.37 m. The rest built up with the scope loosely specified, payments tied to the calendar rather than to completed work, and oversight provided free by a party the owner did not pay.

The owner engaged an independent adviser at month nine, with two months of project remaining. The adviser ran the snag list, the technical handover, the sea trials post-redelivery, and the warranty claim management for the remaining 12 months. Five claims under the yard’s warranty, totalling approximately EUR 410,000, were pursued with the yard and settled within the warranty period.

The adviser’s fee for the engagement was EUR 95,000. The warranty recovery alone was about four times the fee (EUR 410,000 against EUR 95,000). The adviser’s subsequent assessment of the project, in writing for the owner, identified three weaknesses: the loosely specified scope, payments tied to dates rather than completed work, and oversight by the broker that had sold the yacht. The owner’s next refit, at a different yard, was contracted with each of those addressed, and finished within 14 percent of the original quote.
takeaways: Tie milestone payments to defined deliverables (paint cells complete, engine reinstall complete, sea trials passed) rather than to calendar dates.
The owner’s representative on a EUR 5 m refit, paid 4 to 8 percent of project value (EUR 200,000 to 400,000), costs a fraction of an overrun on the scale of this one.
Practitioner contingency reserves of 10 to 25 percent, set by how far the hull has been opened before, cover hidden work; they do not cover a doubling.
Weekly site presence with photographs and a quantified snag list surfaces issues at the point they can still be addressed cheaply.
06-refit.disclosure: Composite of two Foreland project files, 2022 to 2024. Specific yards are not identified. Cost ranges and project durations are within the originals; identifying details adjusted.
06-refit.seoTitle: Refit scope creep: when a EUR 3.2m refit doubled
06-refit.seoDescription: A mid-life refit at a recognised Mediterranean yard. The yard found genuine additional work, and the final cost was double the quote.

07-operations.title: The captain who pushed back.
07-operations.standfirst: Two captain interviews, two days apart, on the same yacht. One candidate agreed with everything. The other pushed back on the owner’s itinerary, the maintenance schedule, and the budget. The owner hired the second. Two years later, the same captain is still on the yacht, and operating cost has run within budget in both seasons.
paragraphs: The owner had taken delivery of a 52 m semi-custom motor yacht 18 months earlier. The first captain, hired through a recruitment agency introduced by the brokerage that sold the yacht, had run the yacht for 14 months before resigning citing “differences in operational philosophy.” The hand-over was orderly. The yacht needed a new captain, and the owner had learned from the first hire.

The owner engaged an independent recruitment agency on his independent adviser’s recommendation. The agency was not introduced by anyone with a continuing commercial relationship with the yacht. The adviser’s advice was that the captain hire was the most consequential decision the owner would make on the yacht, and that the time to do it carefully was now.
Two final candidates emerged from the search. Both had the credentials. Both had worked on similar-sized yachts. Both had references the agency had verified.

The first candidate, a Swedish captain with twelve years of experience, was charming, professional, and accommodating in interview. He agreed with the owner’s preferred itinerary for the upcoming season. He agreed with the owner’s suggestion that the autumn refit period could be “kept tight” to allow for late-season use. He agreed with the recruitment of two crew members the owner’s wife had met socially. The owner left the interview comfortable.

The second candidate, a British captain with fourteen years of experience, was less easy in interview. He pushed back on the proposed itinerary on grounds that the transit times between the owner’s preferred destinations would compromise the yacht’s maintenance schedule. He pushed back on the autumn refit timeline, noting that compressing it would add cost later. He asked detailed questions about how the owner meant to use the yacht, how the family actually behaved on board, and the budget. He noted, politely, that one of the crew the owner’s wife had met socially was not, in his view, the right hire for the role.

The owner’s instinct, after the interview, was to prefer the first candidate. The independent adviser’s view was the opposite. The adviser’s reasoning was that a captain willing to disagree in interview was more likely to disagree later, when it mattered, and that a captain who agreed easily might also agree easily to charter weeks the owner had not planned to release, to refit yards the management company preferred, and to crew the broker had introduced.
The owner hired the second candidate. The decision was uncomfortable at the time, because the owner was choosing the candidate who had disagreed with him.

paragraphs.text: Do not just hire the best captain on paper. Hire the one who can manage you. A good captain runs the yacht. A great captain manages the entire ecosystem around it, including the owner.
paragraphs.attribution: Erica Lay, founder and director, EL Crew Co

paragraphs: Two years on, the captain is still on the yacht. The senior crew he assembled in his first months, the chief officer, chief engineer, chief stewardess and chef, are still aboard. Operating cost has run within the budget agreed at his appointment in both seasons. He has pushed back on yard and supplier proposals where the owner’s budget or programme was at risk, as he had done in interview.
It is too early to put a figure on what the hire has saved. If it shows, it will be in crew retention and budget control, and crew alone is 30 to 40 percent of annual operating cost (chapter 1).

The owner had chosen the first captain mainly on credentials; he chose the second for his judgement. The independent adviser’s view, in conversation, is that the captain hire is the most consequential operational decision an owner makes, and that getting it wrong on the first yacht can cost up to a full year of operating cost.
takeaways: A captain who questions the owner’s plans in interview is showing a quality worth having: a willingness to say what the owner may not want to hear about itinerary, maintenance and budget. Weigh it alongside credentials and references.
Recruit the captain independently, not through the broker or the seller. A captain often keeps a working relationship with whoever introduced them.
Senior crew staying 5 to 8 years is usually a sign of a well-run yacht. An average stay below 2 years usually means the crew are leaving because of the captain or the owner.
The captain’s annual pay is small against the operating cost the captain controls.
07-operations.disclosure: Single Foreland Marine project, 2024 ongoing. Identifying details adjusted; the account of the captain hire and the operating outcomes to date are accurate to the original project.
07-operations.seoTitle: Hiring a superyacht captain: two interviews, two years on
07-operations.seoDescription: Two candidates on the same yacht, two days apart. One agreed with everything. The other pushed back, and got the job.

08-motor-versus-sail.title: The owner who switched, on the second yacht.
08-motor-versus-sail.standfirst: The first yacht was a 48 m motor. The second was a 52 m sailing yacht. The owner had not intended a switch; a written comparison, made when he began looking for a successor, decided it. He is now in his third year on the sailing yacht, and running costs and family use have changed as the comparison suggested they would.

meta.label: Second yacht
meta.value: 52 m sailing yacht, brokerage, year 6 onward

meta.label: Anonymisation
meta.value: Composite of two Foreland project files, 2020 to 2026. Quoted remarks are representative of the files, not verbatim

paragraphs: This account combines two project files. The owner had been on a 48 m motor yacht for five years when the conversation about a successor began. The original acquisition had been straightforward: a brokerage hull from a respected mid-tier German yard, modern and well-specified, sourced through a yacht-management contact. The crew had settled, and family use had settled at seven to nine weeks a year, mostly Western Mediterranean. The annual operating cost ran consistently at EUR 3.9 to 4.2 million.

The successor conversation opened with the assumption that the next hull would be another motor, slightly larger and a little newer. The independent adviser asked whether the comparison had been run against a sailing yacht of the same size band. It had not.
The adviser walked the owner through three documents over the course of two weeks.

The first was an operating-cost projection for a 52 m sailing yacht of comparable build quality, in the same use pattern, run at moderate-use intensity. The model produced an annual figure of approximately EUR 3.0 to 3.2 million, against the EUR 3.9 to 4.2 million the owner had been paying on the motor. The difference came from fuel, a smaller crew and a smaller engine room; against that, the sailing yacht model carried EUR 60 to 90 thousand of annual rigging reserve and a sail wardrobe replacement at the seven-year mark. The sailing yacht would therefore cost about three quarters as much a year as the motor yacht (between 71 and 82 percent at the ends of the ranges). The adviser was clear that the figures were practitioner ranges rather than precise forecasts, but that the difference was larger than the uncertainty in them.

The second was a cruising-calendar comparison. Most of the cost on either yacht was fixed whatever the use, so the adviser did not present the saving as buying weeks. He set out the cost of each week aboard: EUR 430,000 to 600,000 on the motor at seven to nine weeks, against about EUR 190,000 to 230,000 if the family used the sailing yacht for 14 to 16 weeks at its modelled EUR 3.0 to 3.2 million. The owner’s use had been held down partly by the time the family had free and partly by the cost of running a motor yacht at the upper end of moderate use. A lower cost per week reduced the second of these limits.

The third was a rough estimate of carbon emissions. The owner sat on the board of a foundation his family ran, and the foundation had begun publishing its own carbon emissions. On the fuel projections and practitioner figures, switching to a sailing yacht would cut the yacht’s annual carbon emissions from fuel by roughly 60 to 65 percent. The figure mattered to him for reasons that had not been part of the original yacht decision and were now part of the successor decision.

The owner asked the adviser to scope a hybrid motor yacht as a third option. The adviser came back with two delivered Heesen FDHF hulls and one in-build Sanlorenzo SX, modelled at EUR 3.4 to 3.6 million annually. That is about EUR 0.4 million a year more than the sailing yacht and about EUR 0.5 million less than the motor yacht, on the mid-points of the ranges, and the hybrid’s modelled carbon emissions were also between the two. The owner kept the hybrid option open throughout the search.

paragraphs.text: I had thought of sail as a different kind of holiday. The comparison made it look like a different kind of yacht. The two are not the same conversation.
paragraphs.attribution: A remark representative of the owners in the two files, week 14 of the second-yacht search.

paragraphs: The successor was a 52 metre sailing yacht built by Royal Huisman in 2014, on the brokerage market through a Northern European house with no continuing relationship to the owner. The acquisition followed the sequence chapter 9 sets out: independent adviser engaged before any broker, surveyor independently engaged, yacht lawyer drawn from a recognised firm, captain hired through an independent recruitment process and not through the broker.

The captain hired had run two large sailing yachts previously. He pushed back, in interview, on three things the owner had assumed: the owner’s preferred itinerary needed weather windows the family was not used to honouring, the existing motor-yacht crew were not all going to transition to a sailing yacht successfully, and the management company that had run the motor yacht did not have the right depth on sailing yachts. The owner hired him because he had raised these points.

Three of the five senior motor-yacht crew transitioned to the new hull. Two did not. A new chief officer and a new chief engineer were hired with sailing-yacht specialism. A new yacht-management company was engaged.

paragraphs.text: Year three on the new hull

paragraphs: Year three on the sailing yacht is ongoing. The annual operating cost has been EUR 3.0 to 3.2 million, as the model predicted. Family use has run at 13 to 15 weeks a year, against the seven to nine on the motor. The owner reports that the cruising character of the family’s seasons has changed: longer passages between anchorages, more weather-window planning, more time at sea under sail and less time waiting at marinas. The owner’s view is that the sailing yacht suits the way his family lives better than the motor yacht did.

Carbon emissions from fuel have stayed within the modelled range, 60 to 65 percent below the motor yacht’s, and the owner has not had to defend the yacht’s emissions against the foundation’s published figures.

The owner says he would have chosen the hybrid if his cruising calendar had been less flexible. It was not the right yacht for him, but hybrid drive is now a practical third option, and a buyer who compares only motor and sail leaves it out.
takeaways: The motor versus sailing yacht comparison is complete only when the cost projections, the cruising calendar and the carbon emissions are set out in writing.

The crew that suits a motor yacht does not always suit a sailing yacht. Plan for some senior turnover at the transition; budget for hiring sailing specialists rather than expecting the existing crew to adapt.

Hybrid drive is now a practical option. Heesen FDHF, Sanlorenzo SX and similar programmes cost less to run and emit less carbon than a conventional motor yacht, though more than a sailing yacht, and suit owners with fixed cruising schedules.

Choosing the captain is the most important decision at the transition. A candidate willing to question the owner’s assumptions about the calendar, the crew and the management company is worth taking seriously.

09-decision-framework.title: The buyer who walked away.
09-decision-framework.standfirst: Six months of search. Three shortlisted yachts. A surveyed hull at the right yard, at a price the buyer’s adviser considered fair. Then the buyer had his adviser set out how each member of the proposed team would be paid, and every one passed the independence test. He asked one further question, about his own time, and walked away from the acquisition. He has not re-entered the market. He considers the decision the right one.
paragraphs: The buyer was in his late forties, recently exited from a media business, considering a first acquisition in the 45 to 55 m band. He had engaged an independent adviser at the start of the process, and the search had gone smoothly for six months. Three shortlisted yachts. Pre-purchase survey on the preferred candidate. A 49 m motor yacht from a respected mid-tier yard, at EUR 22.5 m, with a clean survey, priced in line with comparable yachts for sale.

The buyer was prepared to close. His lawyer had reviewed the contract. His surveyor had cleared the yacht for purchase. The independent adviser had assembled the team and was prepared to support the closing.

Then the buyer asked the adviser to set out who would advise and work for him over the next decade, what each would be responsible for, and how each would be paid: who by him directly, who only if a deal closed, and who would receive referral fees or retrocessions that he would be paying for indirectly. The adviser took two days to compile the answer.

paragraphs.text: The team, and how each member was paid

paragraphs: The independent adviser, who ran the search, supported the negotiation and assembled the team, was paid by the buyer directly, on a fixed fee. Pass.
The lawyer, who reviewed the purchase contract, was paid by the buyer directly, on a fixed fee. Pass.
The surveyor, who had surveyed the preferred yacht, was paid by the buyer directly. Pass.
The captain candidate, who would run the yacht and lead the crew, had been found through an independent recruitment agency engaged by the adviser and would be paid by the buyer directly. Pass.

The yacht management company, recommended by the adviser from a list of candidates none of which had a continuing relationship with the listing broker, would handle compliance, crew administration and accounts, and would be paid by the buyer directly. Pass.

The insurance broker, selected by the adviser from a panel of three to place the hull and P&I cover, would be paid by a commission included in the premium. This is standard practice; it was disclosed to the buyer in writing, and the adviser judged it acceptable. Pass with disclosure.

The yard for any future refit work was an open question. The adviser noted that, as the buyer meant to cruise mainly in the Western Mediterranean, the natural refit yard would be there, and walked him through the ownership of the main operators there, so that he could apply his independence test to whichever yard he later used.

The buyer asked, separately, about the management company. The adviser noted that of the recognised firms in the over-30 m segment, several had ownership relationships with brokerages the buyer had previously interacted with, and that the firm that best met the six-element independence test was a smaller one the adviser could recommend.

By the end of the conversation, the buyer knew who would work for him, what each would do and how each would be paid. Every fee was disclosed, and every party was either paid by him directly or had disclosed its other payments in writing. The team passed the independence test.

paragraphs.text: The question the fee review did not answer

paragraphs: The buyer asked one further question. He asked his adviser, in private, what proportion of his time, attention, and household conversation the yacht was likely to absorb across the next decade.

The adviser estimated that the yacht would take about 40 to 60 days a year of the buyer’s direct attention, through season planning, refit scheduling, supplier conversations and crew matters, on top of about 80 to 120 days a year of family use. It would also take a large share of household conversation, scheduling and travel arrangements. In the adviser’s view, it would become a centre of gravity in the buyer’s life.

The buyer thanked the adviser. He returned three days later and told the adviser that he had decided not to proceed. His reason was not the team, which had passed every test. The conversation had made him realise that he did not want the yacht to become a centre of gravity in his life.

paragraphs.text: I have spent the last fifteen years building a business that absorbed everything. I have just paid myself for that, and I have a window to choose what comes next. A yacht would be one of the things that comes next. I do not want it to be the largest one.
paragraphs.attribution: The buyer, in conversation with Foreland Marine, week 27.

paragraphs: The buyer’s six-month engagement with Foreland Marine cost approximately USD 110,000 in adviser fees, plus the survey, lawyer, and incidental costs of the search. Total cost of the search that did not result in an acquisition: approximately USD 195,000.

On the book’s figures, owning the 49 m yacht for a decade would have cost approximately USD 42 to 53 m. Operating cost at 12 to 15 percent a year on a price of about USD 25 m (EUR 22.5 m) comes to USD 30 to 38 m over ten years, and the chapter 1 curve puts the loss of value by year ten at 48 to 62 percent, a further USD 12 to 15.5 m. He chose instead a charter relationship that gives him 30 to 40 days a year on similar-grade yachts without owning any of them, at approximately USD 12 to 18 m across the decade, and put the capital the yacht would have tied up into a property programme and a venture investment portfolio. On those ranges the decade costs him approximately USD 24 to 41 m less than ownership would have.

The buyer is an unusual case; most buyers who reach this stage go ahead. The conversation that prompted his decision is not one the trade press tends to publish, but any buyer can have it. Readers are invited to have the same conversation with whichever adviser they are considering, before signing.
takeaways: The independence test, applied to every adviser and to how each is paid, is not the only test. The buyer should also ask how much of the next ten years the yacht will take, and what else that time could be used for. That question rarely leads a buyer to withdraw, but it did here.

Walking away is the sensible response when the buyer’s honest answer about how he will use the yacht is unconvincing. The cost of the search, about USD 195,000 here, is small against a decade of ownership costing USD 42 to 53 m.
Charter, fractional access, and one-off premium charters can deliver 30 to 40 days a year of yacht use without acquisition. For some buyers that is the better choice.
An adviser whose fee does not depend on the purchase going ahead can set out how the whole team is paid and also ask whether the buyer should buy at all.
09-decision-framework.disclosure: Single Foreland Marine project file, 2024. Buyer’s identifying details adjusted. The sequence of the decision, the search cost and the cost comparison with chartering are accurate to the original project.
09-decision-framework.seoTitle: The superyacht buyer who walked away, and why
09-decision-framework.seoDescription: Six months of search, three shortlisted yachts, a surveyed hull at a fair price. Then the buyer asked how much of his time the yacht would take.
